speechtext: Secrecy?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, secrecy. It was not announced. As a matter of fact, it was even denied by agents of COJO. Now
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
an additional fee of $375,000 is paid to Josephson, an American, to negotiate a contract which has to all intents and purposes already been negotiated.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Later, Mr. A1 Eagleson, a well known lawyer from Toronto who had just successfully sold the television package covering the Canada-Russia hockey series, as well as other sports events, protested the fact that an American agent had been given the right to negotiate on behalf of COJO, adding that he as a Canadian would have done it at no cost to COJO. It is ironic that at no time did COJO or ABC or any of the networks seek the services of Mr. Josephson in their negotiations or, for that matter, of any other agent to act on their behalf.
It is imperative that the federal government investigate the connection between the entrance of Mr. Josephson on the scene and the fact that the chief negotiator for the TV rights was one Mr. Paul Desrocher, a well known financial agent for the Quebec Liberal provincial party. Mr. Desrocher, chairman of COJO's subcommittee on television is also, coincidentally, chief organizer for the Quebec Liberal Party and Premier Bourassa's senior adviser. Add to this the fact that it was imperative for Josephson, as a matter of prestige, to secure this coup on behalf of his company, if it was to break into the sports field-something it had never done before-and that the making of money was secondary to the actual gaining of the contracts. This is what he told me face to face in an interview I had with him recently.
In light of this development and my suspicions regarding Josephson based on further comments by numerous sources in Quebec, I took the liberty to write a letter to ABC dated January 30, reading in part as follows:
I believe that at no time were the negotiations conducted by ABC in obtaining the exclusive television rights ever shady or illegal or in any way improper. I do, however, want to reiterate my belief that somewhere along the line, funds did in fact find their way into the Quebec provincial Liberal coffers as a result of the completion of this contract.
Prior to the meeting which was to have been held in Montreal on December 20 and 21, CBS was informed that ABC had signed a contract and that it was pointless for them to show up in Montreal. I have a letter here from the CBS television network signed by the vice-president, Sports, William MacPhail. It reads in part as follows:
In December of 1972 we were informed that a meeting would be held in Montreal with COJO for the purpose of negotiating. Later we were informed that COJO had set dates of December 20 and 21 for these meetings. On December 19 we were informed that a contract had been negotiated and signed between COJO and ABC. In view of this, we deemed it inadvisable to attend the meeting and so informed COJO.
I want to stress the point that Mr. MacPhail makes here in respect of this contract that had been negotiated and signed between ABC and COJO before December 19. Three days previous to this, on December 16, NBC was notified by COJO and ABC had indeed received the rights that all three major U.S. corporations had originally been invited to bid on, yet COJO, weeks after the agreement was finalized, had the audacity to pretend to stage a charade, open-bid meeting knowing as a fact that an agreement had been finalized with ABC. As a result of

March 1, 1974
The Address-Mr. Jelinek
this, NBC sent a long telegram to Lord Killanin, president of IOC, on December 19 outlining their position and their concern regarding the mishandling, in their opinion, of this entire matter. Lord Killanin eventually stated:
Future television negotiations will be conducted jointly by the organizing committee and the IOC board.
We must keep in mind that up to this time the organizing committee has done all the negotiating on its own throughout the history of the Olympics. Then we have the public statement by the vice president of ABC of last Friday, as follows:
If I am to criticize the Montreal organizing committee on any part of it, it would be over not immediately announcing the contract when we reached first agreement almost a month before the announcement.
Much earlier the NBC made the following public statement:
NBC continues to believe that the procedures used to award American television rights to the 1976 Olympic games are contrary to the best interests of the people of Canada, and the American television audience and the games themselves. The organizing committee's unwillingness to follow the procedure of open bidding raises serious questions which are still unanswered.
Finally, on January 3, after all these contradictory statements, a joint announcement was made by COJO and ABC announcing that officially ABC had been awarded the television rights to the 1976 Olympics, notwithstanding the fact that the ABC board of directors in November, 1972, had approved the $25 million fee for Olympic coverage, which also was approved by COJO, subject to certain conditions that had not yet been completely finalized.
In an article published in the Montreal Star in the latter part of January, 1974, serious allegations were made concerning a request of direct payment of money to the Quebec Liberal Party for the rights to negotiate the television contract, as well as an NBC internal decision to bid considerably higher than $25 million. Most assuredly, statements with such serious implications are not made without regard to factual sources and to this end I quote an affidavit by the author of the Montreal Star article. It is as follows:
I, John Robertson, am willing to testify to the accuracy of all statements, including those attributed to others, carried under my byline in the Montreal Star in columns and news stories involving the sale of the North American TV rights to the 1976 Olympic games to the American Broadcasting Company.
Beyond this, Mr. Robertson in his own investigation over the past year has documented evidence to support most of the allegations I have brought forward. His documentation on its own proves beyond doubt that serious irregularities did indeed take place. Statements that moneys did in fact find their way into the Quebec Liberal coffers have been made by more than one source, including numerous statements made to me; but no documented proof regarding this matter has been made available.
To those critics who insist that total proof be brought forward before an inquiry is conducted, let me answer by saying that if we had all the proof, the inquiry in order to get to the full truth would not be necessary. There is just so much that any private individual can do without a public investigation. Quite obviously, I do not have the power to subpoena records and I do not have the power to call witnesses to testify under oath. Without these powers we cannot have definite proof, and a shroud of suspicion

will remain over this entire affair. I have proof, however, that not only did COJO sell the rights to ABC without open bidding; they also gave them a separate agreement guaranteeing that they would be able to match any competitive bid within 30 days in the event bidding did take place.
By far the most serious piece of documented evidence I can provide is the fact that two top officials of COJO as late as December 14, 1972, some weeks after ABC had secretly acquired the rights, personally invited both NBC and CBS to come to Montreal to bid for the rights when indeed they had in fact already been sold. I repeat, the fact that they had planned to conduct this charade is proof enough that COJO tried to cover up after selling the rights secretly in order to create an illusion of open bidding.
The facts here are obvious and speak for themselves. I have made very clear the federal government's responsibility in this matter, particularly as it relates directly to several federal ministries. The contract itself paves the way for an alternate in case of an investigation and the resulting voiding of this contract by either the provincial or the federal government or by COJO itself. The entire matter in which the contract between COJO and ABC was drawn up is more than a little suspect in its make-up.
I have presented this House with documented statements involving serious conflict in times and dates, and I have presented further evidence of statements from the major U.S. television networks. With these documented facts and their surrounding discrepancies, I personally once again call upon the Prime Minister to initiate an immediate investigation, without hindering any progress to the eventual staging of the Olympic games, to once and for all clear up a situation which if left unsolved can only leave each Canadian suspicious of the entire Olympic ideal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the second time since I was elected I have been exposed to a Speech from the Throne, and when I use the word "exposed" I think I allude correctly to the state of affairs in the Liberal Party and the Liberal government. I have the distinct impression that the government has run up to the public, flashed open its trenchcoat to reveal its new clothes but, much like the emperor of the Hans Anderson fairy-tale, there is nothing to show-indeed, not even the bare essentials.
The crisis of the cost of living in this country requires more substance than has been offered. For instance, it is not adequate that the government promises "reasonable food prices" when prices have been steadily rising without government intervention. The people in my riding are suffering now, never mind tomorrow. I shall read some letters which I have received from constituents over the past two weeks, to give hon. members an idea what people are up against in a real way at this time. These are the real problems, not the problems of the ivory tower where unresponsive, indecisive, banal cliches are rolled out like so much confederate money. I should like to take this opportunity during the debate on the Speech from the Throne to give real voice to the feelings of the people of my constituency.
March 1, 1974

Mrs. Valerie Barry of Nickel Centre wrote to me as follows:
I have never before this year regarded myself or my family as being poor as we have found this year. I have two children and there are thousands of people who have considerably larger families. My husband quite often works 14-16 hour days and yet I cannot afford to buy the proper kinds of food for my family. At one time if you wanted fancy foods, you expected to pay high prices for them. Now we cannot afford staples. Speaking for my own family, I have not purchased any beef for three months at least. The reason being by the time we buy bread, milk, potatoes and other groceries there is not any money left for steak or pork chops or things that I feel every Canadian has a right to. We live in the richest country in the world and yet we are deprived of eating proper diet due to ridiculous prices. As our representative, I hope that perhaps you can help us by at least working to give Mrs. Plumptre's committee some authority to get us some changes.
Mr. McCaughey, from Garson, writes to say:
Dear Sir:
Re the high cost of living, here is one who is very concerned with it. The Prime Minister doesn't seem to care what becomes of the voters. They will be too weak from malnutrition to get out and vote if this continues.
Instead of bread going up, why not hard liquor, cigars and cigarettes. Children eat bread, not liquor. I am on a fixed income, but I did get a raise on the Canada pension. I can get along, but it's one raise after another on staples that worries me. Why not bring the cost of living down, and then they wouldn't need to hand out these raises and everyone would benefit.
Here is a letter from someone who signs himself, or herself, "A plea for help":
Dear Sir:
Just took a few moments to sit down and write you this letter about trying to raise and feed a family of six children plus two adults. To feed and clothe, upkeep of a home is almost impossible. Sure they say that prices are according to your take home pay. Well, I say baloney to that.
Just for one instance, let's take food, which everyone needs to survive, and I don't mean steak, just a simple pot of home-made beans for a family of eight. My husband paid for 12 packages of 14 oz. (less than a pound each) $6.33 December 27, 1973, less than two months ago. And I can assure you that is used up in no time at all. Weston split-peas, one package, 16 oz., 51 cents, which was 36 cents less than a month ago. Also rice, white sugar just to name a few; also potatoes which are the main vegetable on the table.
As you have a family of your own to raise, I am sure that you will agree with me that it is a hardship to manoeuvre with no relief in sight. Even people with no children have difficulty in making ends meet where food is concerned. Clothes can be made out of hand-me-downs, or purchased at the Salvation Army, but there is no substitute for food.
Either eat or starve. We have a choice. In closing, I hope that this letter will be joined with many more in this same situation that we are in trying to raise and feed a family.
This is a letter from Mrs. Katherine Thomas of Val Caron:
This price increase is completely ridiculous. We all have heard it is caused by world food supplies. I am sorry, but I am worried about my family. It is getting harder and harder to feed my children healthy, nutritious meals when my husband's wages don't keep up with the rise in the costs of food and clothing for children. If it is hard on us with a comparatively good wage, what are the senior citizens and people classified as "poor" eating?
Please help and do something about it. Your party out of all can, with the balance of power, even if it brings an election. Maybe if an election is going to be called, a lot of things will come more clearer.
Mrs. Plumptre can't do anything and unfortunately is taking a lot of criticism which should be against the politicians who could do something but apparently don't care.
The Address-Mr. Rodriguez
Sugar has gone up terribly, white beans, spaghetti and eggs. Good heavens, I am sure all these don't depend on anchovies off the Peruvian coast.
Take action now or I am positive the next election will prove that this is the major point in the voters' minds.
Mrs. Jennie Williamson, of Naughton, Ontario, writes as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am writing in regard to the high cost of living. My husband is a pensioner; he is 67, I am 60. We also have a 16-year old boy attending Lively high school.
As I'm sure you must know, groceries have gone "sky high". White sugar has risen from $1.43 for ten pounds to $2.54 since last fall. Honey has gone from 89 cents to $2.09. Now, how much more does it cost to keep bees today than it did three or four years ago?
I believe Dominion Stores showed a profit of 90 per cent, the highest of any chain store. Why is there not more investigating in this regard.
I would like to know what Mrs. Plumptre is doing. How could anyone on $40,000 know anything about the needs of a family on less than $5,000? What a waste of $40,000. Why can the tax not be eliminated on all clothing? Also essentials like toilet paper, soaps, cleaners, etc. My husband (Earl) worked hard all his life, and never drew unemployment insurance in his life and was never unemployed and had to retire at 62 because he has trouble with his back and legs.
Please try to do something to try to raise pensions and bring down the cost of living.
Yours truly,
Again, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the end of my address I will entertain questions. I might point out to the House that this is the people of Canada speaking, and when the people of Canada are speaking I think it important they be on the record of the House of Commons.
Then, from Mrs. Sylvia Cheviette of Sudbury I have this letter which is addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
Dear Mr. Trudeau:
As the head of our country you must get plenty of complaints, but I must add one more. Isn't there anything you can do to stop the increases in all prices? All companies and stores seem to have great profits when they give out their figures. The feeds are going up for animals, fertilizers also. This means the farmer can't afford to keep a farm, and with many of them going out of business we will in a few years time have a lot less food. We have potatoes in the Valley and other areas, and when they go into our stores they charge the same that they charge for P.E.I. or N.B. potatoes. How can the prices be the same? I've spoken to some farmers and they say they don't get the difference, so where does it go?
Milk went up from 22 cents a can to 26 cents. Sugar has gone up from $1.59 to $2.69 for ten pounds, bread also. These are just a few and it's getting worse all the time. Soon we won't be able to eat because we will be getting a stub with no amount on the cheque as the deductions are getting bigger, and then the money you do get can't be stretched all that far because the prices are getting impossible.
Please take some kind of action before we are unable to eat at all.
This is a letter from the Waters women's institute in Waters township.

March 1, 1974
The Address-Mr. Rodriguez
Dear Sir:
We are very concerned about the abrupt rise in prices for the following food items: sugar, white beans, soda biscuits, rice. We would like to have the Food Prices Review Board investigate why the prices have risen on items mentioned and if possible an answer in the news media of what they discover.
Next is a letter from Mrs. Joan Callack, of Whitefish in my riding:
Dear Sir:
It's been on my mind for a long time, I thought it's about time I did something about it, or perhaps you can do something about the problem of high prices on food, clothing, etc., etc.
My husband works every day, has a steady job, yet all we get out of his wages is our roof over our heads and groceries that last from one payday to the next, and barely at that.
We have four children, one of which attends secondary school in the next community. Also, he turned 18 years of age one month ago. We are not able to clothe this student decently. Youth allowance did help, kept him in jeans, but $20 does not buy a very good pair of shoes, though. We are doing our best but it's just not doing very good.
The next letter is from Mrs. Harrison of Chelmsford:
Dear Sir:
I would like to know when is it going to end, the price of food going up. Every time we're going to the store, it's gone up. Something must be done. All we hear is talk, but nothing being done.
Here is a letter from Mrs. G. F. Maxam of Garson:
Dear Mr. Rodriguez:
... I wish to say how disturbed I am at the rising cost of living, especially food. No doubt you will be inundated with mail concerning this state of affairs.
My husband will be retiring this spring, and although some but not all provisions are made for our welfare, I and many others wonder when it will all end. Granted, there will be only two of us, but there are those with four to six children who will find it very difficult.
Here is a letter from Mrs. Rowland of Val Caron in my riding:
Dear Mr. Rodriguez:
... We are very concerned about the rising prices on everything. I am sending you a copy of the letter I am sending Mrs. Plumptre in Ottawa, and how about going down there and trying to check things up and get an investigation going or something to bring those prices down so we can live a decent life?
Here is a letter from Ray Lagare of Val Therese, Ontario:
I would like to write a few lines to you concerning the high cost of living. In a country as wealthy as ours there is no food shortage as emphasized by the government. Some items in the large chain stores are up as much as 300 per cent in a short while, but our wages will go up a small 3V2 per cent on the 10th of July. How can we manage with a family when the cost of living is increasing steadily at such a fast rate?
I think that you should stand in the House with your colleagues and tell Mr. Lewis that he has given the Liberals enough time to look at the situation through their famous Mrs. B. Plumptre and her prices review board.
I am sure the Canadian people are fed up with this kind of beating around the bush while the prices are skyrocketing.
And so the letters come from individuals and from organizations. On the other hand, all these people are aware that while they struggle to buy food and survive on their income, the food companies and other corporations in this country are not forced to engage in the same struggle. The Weston company, with its finger in the Loblaw "By gosh, the price is right" pie shows an increase in profit of

more than 80 per cent. Profits for the Canada Packers and Schneider's companies are up 36 per cent and 45 per cent respectively. Dominion Stores' profits were up 30 per cent over the nine months period ending December 15.
Even Mrs. Plumptre is starting to tell the consumer some disturbing things, as in the case of the unjustified increases in the price of bread. But I need not enumerate all these, for the profits increases situation in this country has reached the point where it has become a personal affront to every Canadian who is living on a fixed income, a low wage, a middle-level income or those who are unemployed.
This is where the term "free enterprise" becomes a rather interesting description of the system under which we are living. Free enterprise for whom? No one but the companies. While the Conservatives pay homage to free enterprise on the one hand, they propose on the other hand to institute wage and price freezes. They do not propose a profit freeze but, rather, would simply freeze the prices at their inflated levels and freeze the already inadequate wages of the working people who cannot cope with prices as they are-and this despite the experience in Britain and the United States.
Not only have the companies of this country benefited from the corporate welfare lumped on them by the Liberal government, and the Conservative government before them, but they have now wrapped up the free enterprise corner in such a way as to trap the Canadian people. Where is the free enterprise in having no control over the wages coming into your pocket for a hard day of work? Where is the free enterprise in having no control over the expenditure of that money? Where is the free enterprise in paying out every cent to keep food in the body and a roof over a family?
In return for having to pay to exist, can we look around and say that this level of existence is for a good cause? Can we assure ourselves that the poor are being helped, that our aged and our disadvantaged are living decent lives, that our children will be free to pursue their own goals because of the planning that is being done today? Can we look around and find just one group of people who are benefiting from this crisis other than the directors who sit on the boards of the companies whose profits are skyrocketing?
What is this story that nothing can be done? Surely, while a part of inflation is imported, the elected representatives on this country have the brains collectively to resolve a major portion of the country's current problems. Surely, it is not enough to admit that the government is capable of administering during the booms but incapable of governing through the lower periods or the busts. The capability to govern does not exist unless it exists and works in times of crisis such as now.
Now I would like to turn my attention to my own area, generally speaking. What about the issue which the Prime Minister said in 1968 he would strive to eliminate, namely, regional disparity? Here we are, six years later and umpteen throne speeches later-the latest one on Wednesday of this week-and what is said about regional development? The throne speech contains only one line on the matter which is as follows: "The government attaches great importance to regional development".
March 1, 1974

I live in and represent a regionally underdeveloped area in northern Ontario, Nickel Belt. Indeed, all of northern Ontario is considered a regionally underdeveloped area. This area has 12 representatives in the House. In 1968, 11 of the 12 were Liberals. Today, nine of the 12 are members of the governing party with specific and responsible positions. One is a cabinet minister, one is chairman of the Liberal caucus, one is deputy whip, and several are chairmen of standing committees or parliamentary secretaries.
We who live in northern Ontario are well aware of the regional disparity between our part of the province and other parts of this country, and indeed the southern part of Ontario. It is a fair comment to make that northern Ontario exists as a colony subject to a centralist administration in Toronto and a monstrously unresponsive government in Ottawa. I have often heard it said that northern Ontario has been the backbone of federal Liberal support in Ontario. Why then do you continue to treat us in northern Ontario as the backside of Canada?
Neither is the Ontario government exempt from the responsibility of developing northern Ontario. After all, out of the 16 provincial seats in northern Ontario, the Tories hold eight, with several cabinet ministers among them. But in case you think I overstate the problem, I draw the attention of the House to the Toronto centred region plan prepared for the provincial government and accepted by the Tories as official government policy. The Toronto centred region plan states:
There are certain reasons for the centre of development being in the Toronto centred region. They are primarily
(i)	the primacy of Toronto in social, economic and cultural life,
(ii)	the relation with other major cities in Canada, especially
Montreal,
(iii)	the relation to the major markets in the United States,
(iv)	the manufacturing of the resources from northern Ontario and
distribution to United States markets ...
The Toronto centred region population will reach eight million by 2000 A.D.
The Toronto centred region will remain the financial, manufacturing, cultural and communications centre of Ontario and Canada, and will relate primarily to the United States.
There it is, the official view of northern Ontario as seen by the Tories who rule us from Toronto. We who live here know that northern Ontario is the repository of the mineral wealth of Ontario and indeed of Canada, yet the share of the work force in secondary manufacturing is well below the provincial and national levels. We do not have oil, but we have uranium owned by that great Tory who ran for the Conservative Party federally and was defeated. He spent $92,000.
About 30 per cent of the northern Ontario work force is employed in forestry or mining. The remaining 70 per cent is involved in the service industry. This is below the accepted ratio for service employment to other employment. Even the growth prospects under present circumstances are appalling. In the period 1966 to 1970, according to the provincial department of natural resources, mineral wealth increased approximately 70 per cent, while employment in that field increased by 5.3 per cent. This is corroborated by the Economic Council of Canada, which states that the projected growth of mining employment has been estimated to be marginally less than the growth of mining production. Indeed, Mr. J. Edward Grubb, presi-
The Address-Mr. Rodriguez
dent of INCO, speaking a few months ago in New York, stated that last year, 1973, production at INCO's operation will be accomplished by mining the highest quality ore now; in other words, high-grading ore.
Inco did it, going from a work force of 18,000 in January, 1972, to a work force of 13,000 by the end of 1973, and with its profits up 100 per cent to a whopping $227 million. Falconbridge, the other "godfather" in the Sudbury basin, had a 770 per cent increase in 1973. Indeed, when one reads what the resource industries have made in northern Ontario one is left breathless when considering the underdevelopment in that part of the country. The Abitibi company had an increase of 260 per cent, and Noranda Mines 75 per cent.
What about the federal government's view of northern Ontario? Look at the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It was set up in 1968 and was headed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) at a time when the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) was minister of transport. They have been playing a game of musical chairs. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion said the following to the Standing Committee on Regional Development, on April 10, 1973, four years after DREE had been established and northern Ontario had been designated as a special area:
Northern Ontario has experienced a growth rate in population of less than 1 per cent per year throughout the decade of the 1960s, slightly below the average for the Atlantic region. It tends to be characterized by a dual economy comprising urban centres such as Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury, North Bay and Timmins, where incomes are at or above national averages, and rural and remote areas and resource towns, where incomes tend to be substantially below the Canadian average and where economic growth depends almost entirely upon primary resource production.
The general social and economic climate in northern Ontario suggests that special efforts will be required if there is to be a significant increase in the employment and value of production derived from the extensive natural resource base and an increase in the viability of some of the urban centres.
As recently as this week the minister announced the signing of a general development agreement with the province of Ontario in which it is stated-and this is what we have to look forward to in northern Ontario:
Other subsidiary agreements involving regions within northern Ontario are under discussion. The first of these is for northwestern Ontario and is a regional economic package which might include resource development roads, an industrial complex feasibility study and infrastructure in selected growth centres. A second will pertain to northeastern Ontario.
We have had the study route, Mr. Speaker. Thousands upon thousands of studies have been done on how we can diversify secondary industry and undertake development in northern Ontario. That is all I have heard since coming to this place. The problem has been studied to death. The time has come for action.
One of the themes we got from DREE last year was on decentralization. But what have we found since? We have found that DREE is not decentralized into northern Ontario. As a matter of fact, it is recentralized into Toronto. Anybody who has lived in northern Ontario knows the bias displayed by northern Ontarians toward southern Ontarians. To centralize an office of DREE in
94

March 1, 1974
The Address-Mr. Rodriguez
Toronto, supposedly to help develop northern Ontario, shows crass treatment of the situation. Indeed, the government's concluding observation in its interdepartmental report regarding DREE's performance in northern Ontario specifically states at page 10:
In light of these circumstances special efforts may be required to strengthen existing resource industries, encourage diversification where viable opportunities exist, and assist in the social adjustment process for those who choose to leave the communities.
The federal government ought to be looking at policies which would develop northern Ontario industrially. In this light a minerals policy which would provide for the establishment of a national minerals corporation, that would take into its portfolio the resources of Ontario, particularly northern Ontario, so that their development could take place for the benefit of our people, would be a great help. There are many reasons why our resources should be owned by the people. These include the creation of employment, the provision of revenue so that the quality of life can be improved for the people who live in the region where the resource is located and who help to mine and produce it and, thirdly, through public ownership of our resources we can maintain our economic independence.
In 1972 the Science Council of Canada released a number of reports dealing with innovations and the structure of Canadian industry. I quote from Study No. 23, which was one of the background studies for the council, as follows:
Canada's great area of strength lies in its natural resources. With competition as keen as it is in the world today, each country must seek to take maximum advantage of those areas in which it has some comparative advantage. This, however, must not be interpreted to mean that we should further accelerate our already precipitous rate of resource extraction. Unquestionably this latter approach, coupled with massive infusions of foreign capital, could keep our GNP rising for a number of years; but before the children of today could reach middle age most of the resources would be gone, leaving Canada with a resource-based economy and no resources.
Our resources must be used as a lever in the industrial development of the province and to add more value to mined resources before exporting them. There is no coincidence in the fact that our resources, by and large, are controlled by foreign corporations and that there is little product development in the province or indeed in the country. I quote further from the same Science Council report:
Alcan does a large part of its product development in the U.K., Inco does most of its product development in the U.S., Johns Manville ... all of its asbestos development in the U.S., Andy and Harmon ... silver product development in the U.S., and Engelhart... all research on platinum is performed in the U.S.
The Science Council continues:
Therefore, in order to succeed in building on our resources, it will be necessary to correct this very fundamental weakness. It will be essential for Canada to develop and exercise product engineering and design capability, and this at all levels, from end product to resource.

The private sector has failed to do what is necessary, that which not only I but the Science Council of Canada believe is critical if we are to create employment in manufacturing industries in parts of the country like my own. As long as the corporations are allowed to exploit our resources with the goal of maximizing their profits, they will never voluntarily create a viable secondary industry in this province or in this country.
Secondly, I think the government ought to consider. developing northern Ontario as one special area, providing infrastructure in all municipalities where development is needed. Thirdly, often when incentives are considered, we think of incentives to corporations and business. We never think of incentives to individuals except when we want them to move from one part of the country to another. I think incentives should be given to individuals living in northern Ontario, for example, through a graduated taxation system. Such graduated tax scales could include sales taxes, personal income tax, OHIP premiums, etc. In some areas of northern Ontario there should be no gasoline tax.
Combined with incentives to individuals there should be disincentives to the wealthier parts of the province and the country, for example, southern Ontario. Those disincentives could take the form of taxation on primary resource exports, higher freight rates on shipping raw material out of the north and very cheap rates on shipping the finished product to some market.
The idea of transportation, Mr. Speaker, leads me to my fourth point. There is no reason in the world why my part of the country, northern Ontario, should be the highest freight rate area in the country. Between Levis, Quebec, and Armstrong, northern Ontario, freight rates on the CNR are the highest in the country. On the provincial government's railway, the ONR, freight rates were cut by 18 per cent. This government ought to instruct the CNR that they should cut the freight rates on that line, and ship the finished products out of northern Ontario, by the same percentage. It is interesting to note that it is much cheaper to ship raw materials out of northern Ontario than it is to ship finished products. One example is iron ore pellets. It costs $8.60 to ship a ton of iron ore pellets from Copper Cliff to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; but if you were to ship a ton of fertilizer to Toronto from Sudbury it would cost $90.80 per ton. These discrepancies can only serve to lock us into being hewers of wood and drawers of water for time immemorial.
Mr. Speaker, I make a fifth proposal to the government of an over-all industrial strategy for northern Ontario. There is no over-all industrial strategy. It seems to be always on an ad hoc basis, with the north condemned forever to being the receptacle of the raw resources. My sixth proposal is that we need a comprehensive and cohesive transportation policy in northern Ontario. We cannot have Air Canada dropping out of service from Sudbury to Timmins, or Sudbury to North Bay, without replacing that service with some kind of comprehensive program where transportation for moving people around my part of the country would be enhanced and facilitated.
Mr. Speaker, lastly I propose to the government a permanent secretariat for development in northern Ontario.
March 1, 1974

This secretariat would be resident in northern Ontario and it would comprise provincial and federal personnel from the area. There ought to be an ongoing body which would oversee development in northern Ontario and to which the people of northern Ontario could apply for redress or improvement in their living conditions.
These are only some of the proposals I make to the government with respect to development in northern Ontario which has been sadly neglected over the past 100 years. I remind the government benches that the Prime Minister was very concerned about eradicating regional disparities. We have very serious problems with respect to regional disparity, and I think it is time they were looked at. It is obvious that members on the government side who represent this area have not been raising the issues.
With regard to the pipeline, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) recently came to northern Ontario with some minions from the area and suggested a review of the route of the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal. That is just a palliative to the people of northern Ontario. The decision was made by the cabinet. Mr. Speaker, I call on them to reconsider that decision in light of the kind of development that can take place in northern Ontario. We have been ignored too long. I call on the government to pay attention to the present situation and to take action now to correct some of these discrepancies.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to congratulate His Excellency the Governor General and thank him for having accepted his new responsibilities in that public service spirit that he has shown throughout his extraordinary career. As for Her Excellency Mrs. Leger, who always admirably supported her husband, we already see the stamp of her extraordinary readiness of wit and of the great warmth of personality in everything she has undertaken during the short time she has discharged her duties.
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
I hope I may also express the great satisfaction I find in seeing again Mr. Speaker in the Chair to preside over our debates. He shows great ability and tactfulness in the fulfilment of his duty. He succeeds in moderating our debates. He even manages to curb the eagerness for criticism which is of course the essential part of this House, provided those criticisms do not in their overzealousness, go beyond their purpose, which is to serve the people. The Speaker helps a great deal to bring our debates to the level required by the high responsibility of this House. I am also delighted to find around him the team that supports him and contributed so much to the success of the last session, which is of good omen for the session we shall now go through.
It is in accordance with the usual practice to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I must say that I am doing so today most sincerely and not only to comply with a practice of this House.
They demonstrated with exceptional eloquence their concern for the welfare of all those we are here to serve, and behaved in the best of parliamentary traditions.
While'listening to them, I could not refrain from thinking that the backbenchers on this side of the House are filled with talents and, like the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I find this very encouraging and feel that, as long as the Canadian people is willing to assure us of its trust, this party in the House has the necessary personnel to come up to its expectations.
The extraordinary contributions of our members to the proceedings of the committees of the House is ample proof of this. I have been told that 77 hon. members took part in 626 meetings of the parliamentary committees which were created and in operation during the last session. Mr. Speaker, that means exceptional regularity of attendance made necessary, of course, by the existence of a minority government. The parliamentarians from this side of the House met that great challenge with honour and deserve to be lauded for their sense of service and fellowship.
They have decided to serve their constituents here although, as many of us, they would have liked to be with them more often. All of us in Parliament have suffered from not being able to communicate with our constituents as much as we would have liked.
As far as I am concerned, during the session, I had to cancel four or five meetings that had been organized in my riding in order to fulfil my parliamentary obligations. Of course I did so most regretfully, but parliamentary duty came first. You will tell me that Parliament is in minority for everybody and that my remarks are irrelevant but I would like to remind you that absences do not have the same effect for the opposition as for Cabinet members, who are vested with the initiative right of government and with the responsibility of parliamentary stability.
Our duty was undoubtedly to be here, in the House, I admit it. But is parliamentarism better served by the attitude of the opposition which takes advantage of circumstances, with many members being absent one day and reappearing the next day in number in order to force,
27398-7J

March 1, 1974
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
through mean calculations, Cabinet members to be isolated from their constituents?
For if our duty lies clearly within this Chamber, it is also very important as far as the people are concerned, since we have the responsibility of maintaining contacts with the people who have elected us, of consulting them on the way they would like us to conduct the affairs of state and since we have the duty to inform them of what is happening in the House of Commons, because we are not working here for us but for them.
The Member of Parliament, the parliamentarian is so much more efficient in the House of Commons as he has the opportunity from time to time to go back to those who have elected him in order to try to understand what their aspirations are.
As a new parliamentarian, I must admit that every time I have had the opportunity of meeting the people, when I accepted to speak before a few groups, I was always enhanced and renewed by these experiences, for it is obvious that a politician is renewing only at the source of his mandate. Voters are the source of his mandate. He has the duty and the responsibility of maintaining contacts with voters.
The situation of the minority government, mainly the situation created by the opposition party, certainly prevented us from discharging this portion of our responsibilities. Because it is not as some like to say that it is by sitting on the opposition benches that one renovates oneself politically speaking. This is obvious after a session such as this one, when one sees that the opposition parties did not succeed since it is said that they are in the best possible situation to renew themselves. They did not succeed in suggesting coherent measures to deal with the problems we are facing.
But it is because, in spite of difficulties, we have kept government initiative that we still have the right, during this second session, to keep on governing.
I would like to deal very briefly with another aspect of opposition and namely that of parliamentary holidays. I do not know of any Parliament in the world sitting as long as ours. Under conditions which we all know, the opposition took advantage of our minority situation to make our task even more difficult. For example, by ignoring the school vacations, they have pursued sterile debates to try and break the morale of hon. members who saw the days passing by without being able to take turns as the opposition members did and spend some time with their families.
Particularly in Canada, the size of which is such a geographical challenge, an agreement should allow those of us from both ends of the country to meet our family obligations. The children of those hon. members have the same rights as other children and I am convinced that Parliament could meet this reality if it were not for the prejudicial game of the opposition members.
Some hon. members made the sacrifice of their holidays which they had scheduled with their family and I still remember one of them saying during a meeting:

It means a lot to me, but I would give it up because I know that this government has maintained its will to govern.


However, Mr. Speaker, these are situations about which we should agree so that it may be possible at least to practice this profession, which is a great one, in somewhat better conditions. I hope that the opposition has come to the end of this hide-and-seek strategy and that during this second session it will consider the House as a place of work rather than a trap to grasp power.
In this House, we discuss bills, but we can do it well only if we refer to what the people are thinking. To be able to do so, we must go among the people from time to time.
My main objective, Mr. Speaker, is of course to tell my colleagues about the part of the Speech from the Throne which deals with my department and, with your permission, I shall now talk about the business of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology and, more specifically, about the intention expressed in the Speech from the Throne to reinforce the mandate of this department.
The foundation of liberalism has always been to remain within the path of history and to favour a concentration, based upon circumstances, on the natural forces of society for the advance of humanity. From that point of view, scientific activity played a leading part and was one of the major forces in the changes since the last war.
Over the past decade, the awareness of the impact of science and technology on evolution has led us, and ours is not the only country, to re-examine that area of government expenditures. Even here, in Canada, numerous studies have been initiated on this problem. Among others, there was the Glassco Commission whose terms of reference did not include this but however it did consider that problem, the Mackenzie report, the Gendron report and, more recently, the Senate investigation on scientific policy presided by hon. Senator Maurice Lamontagne. The OECD has also initiated studies on the impact of science and technology on changes. It is perhaps the results or impact of major scientific research programs of the major industrial countries which have drawn attention on this area of government expenditures.
Arising from the success of those scientific programs which were called "Big Science", many countries have set up, as we did, a department whose function is to coordinate the research endeavours within the country and to make those endeavours contribute to the national objectives. In this respect, we ought to congratulate Senator Lamontagne for having conducted his inquiry with such strength, in spite of many criticisms at times, for in some circles what he was trying to do was very little understood, and for having wanted to make the whole country understand with this inquiry how important was the scientific activity. Senator Lamontagne's report represents six years of hearings during which groups interested in this area of activity have submitted briefs and made their opinions known. The hon. senator has published many works in which he has given us an exhaustive analysis of the state of science and technology in Canada and by which he has made us able to make comparisons with some other countries, since it was somewhat difficult to assess objectively, without any point of comparison, whether what we are doing is consistent with what is
March 1, 1974

going on in other countries. He gave us the opportunity to compare with other countries. Moreover, because of his familiarity with the Canadian situation, he pointed out the weaknesses of our research network, whether inside government, in the universities or the industry, as well as the mechanisms linking this research network. The interest given by Senator Lamontagne to this question has surely contributed to the establishment of the ministry, and even today, through his studies, he has thrown much light on the ways and means to fulfill our mandate of Minister of State for Science and Technology.
Naturally, this study was a comprehensive revision of all government spending activities and this reviewing process has, in certain circumstances, troubled somewhat the scientific community. It is understandable that it should fear changes-everyone does-that it should question its necessity, that it should be afraid that new directions will disturb its projects. But in my opinion, the scientific community is in a better position to accept revision, because it is for scientists a professional fact-of-life in a way. It is the essence of scientific activity, and for this reason we have carried on this re-evaluation at a sufficiently slow pace and with great confidence, because we are certain of being understood by the scientific community. Of course, during that reassessment, we have held many consultations and I had the opportunity on several occasions to appear before groups of researchers to explain specifically what the government intends to do under the mandate granted to the Ministry of State for Science and Technology.
In the Speech from the Throne, the government is reasserting its intention of carrying out some recommendations of Senator Lamontagne and taking the necessary steps for the development of a scientific policy in Canada.

In the 1960s the world witnessed a dramatic growth of scientific activity. The international scientific race had begun, and with it realization that any concerted effort in scientific research must be tied to national goals. It was a new philosophy that was injected into the scientific activity whereby scientists were allowed to go about doing their own little thing. It became apparent that governments had to look to scientists to help solve problems of modern society. Good ideas to solve problems are not sufficient, or even useful, by themselves. Their impact has to be researched and their course prolonged into the future so we will know exactly to what that good idea will lead us. In that process, of course, new ideas will emerge in many cases which are related to the kinds of solutions for which we are looking.
Governments face the responsibility of studying the different options available to them. We now know that several options arise in the solutions to certain problems which face modern society. We can choose which options suit us best. Governments now have the responsibility to set up a mechanism by which they will be in a better position to make those choices. We now choose our futures because we have many futures ahead of us. However, we must set up the machinery to make those choices adequately. It is in order to be in a better position that the government is now suggesting the mandate of MOSST be
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
reinforced. I quote a portion of the Speech from the Throne:
The development and use of technology is also essential to the government's approach to increasing national economic production. Steps will be taken to obtain greater returns from industrial research and development as well as technological innovation in Canada.
Scientific knowledge and its application is a keystone to meeting the challenges facing Canada, including those in the areas of food, energy or industrial development. The objective of the government's science policy is the rational generation and acquisition of scientific knowledge and the planned use of science and technology in support of national goals. The Ministry of State for Science and Technology will be developing national science objectives as a basis for exercising enhanced advisory and co-ordinating authority within the government. Two new granting councils will be formed, one for social sciences and humanities and the other for natural sciences.
Certain profound and important changes in public attitude toward science and technology have taken place since the 1960s. For a long time science and technology were fields which the taxpaying public supported without asking too many questions. The relationship between the taxpayer and the scientist was similar to that of a patient toward his doctor. If that relationship has changed, so has the relationship of the public toward the scientist. Taxpayers and politicians alike are no longer as prepared to finance increased scientific expenditures without the opportunity of closer public scrutiny of their activities and of participating in the decisions related to this activity. In some areas this is often perceived as a threat to science; it is perceived as a possible intention of brigading science into meeting government or political objectives.
I reiterate that the whole mandate of the ministry does not mean there is a denial of financial assistance nor of the importance of curiosity-oriented research. Nor is it a repudiation of the basic freedom of the scientist to choose his own field of research. It is a recognition of the high level of government involvement in financing research and development programs.
The people of Canada expect, and rightly so, that scientific resources should be used to solve problems of national concern. The concerns of the people and their representatives must increasingly become the concerns of the scientific community. Subjects such as environmental protection and alternate sources of energy are fields that can have a profound effect on the quality of life and are thus examples of areas where increased attention by the scientific community is indicated.
The science policy cannot be confined to specialists, be they scientists or legislators. The whole population must enter the debate. They must participate in the different choices we will want to make. In proposing these measures, we are attempting to reinforce the mandate of the ministry. We are attempting to balance the needs of the public with needs to maintain and enhance a viable and productive research and development sector within Canada.
Science policy has been described in the throne speech as "the rational generation and acquisition of scientific knowledge and the planned use of science and technology in support of national goals." This is at the base of the mandate of the ministry. As the throne speech indicates, my ministry is to have a strengthened role. Its advice will increasingly be taken into account by cabinet in relation to policies dealing with scientific and technical concerns,

March 1, 1974
The Address-Mrs. Sauve
many of which will originate from operating departments while others will obviously be initiated within the ministry. Its impact will also be markedly increased in relation to the assessment of scientific programs and associated expenditures.
An arrangement has been worked out between the ministry and treasury board so that the ministry will be provided in advance with full information of scientific expenditures of the various departments. It will have a chance to review and assess these expenditures and it will have the responsibility of giving its advice to treasury board. Just as important, this process will lead me to publish a report on scientific expenditures at the same time as the main estimates, so that the public at large may have an opportunity to discuss those expenditures. This will afford an opportunity for all those interested in doing so to enter into discussion as to the direction expenditures in connection with science should be taking. We will develop guidelines concerning these expenditures and advise individual departments as well as treasury board in connection with specific programs. Publication of this report will offer one of the primary means of analysis.
I should like to say something about the co-ordinating mandate given to the ministry under the terms of which, when a specific area of research does not fall clearly under one department, the Minister of State for Science and Technology is called upon to act as a co-ordinating mechanism so that the departments concerned can get-together in a multi-disciplinary fashion. Our purpose is to ensure that federal scientific resources are used in the best possible way for the betterment of the quality of life in Canada. Basically, what the Speech from the Throne is saying is that the role of the ministry is being reinforced by the review assessment arrangements which have been made between ourselves and treasury board. As applied to research being carried out inside government, the objective is to ensure more cohesion and avoid overlapping.
The government also subsidizes outside research, and this comes under the same general mandate. The ministry will be asked to suggest means of improving funding structures. It will be asked to provide a definition of the roles of the National Science Council, the Science Council of Canada and the Defence Research Board. We have suggested the creation of new granting councils so as to correct imbalances between various disciplines.
Since time is running out, I think I should address myself to an area of scientific research which a number of studies have categorized as the weakest inside government. I am speaking of research and development grants in the field of applied research. Canada does grant more money for fundamental research than it does for applied research, and the imbalance will have to be corrected. This does not mean we shall deprive one sector for the sake of the other. If we do have something good going for us, that is to say an outstanding capability in fundamental research, my firm belief is that we should maintain it. Certainly, though, special attention will need to be paid to the field of applied research. Studies have shown that industrial research and development is weakest relative to other areas of endeavour, and this weakness has probably led to our poor performance in the area of high technology.

I think the hon. member who spoke before me made reference to this point, and a question on precisely this subject was directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would offer the congratulations of all my constituents to His Excellency Governor General Jules Leger and to Madame Leger. I trust good health will be afforded them so they will be able to devote their lives to enhancing the spirit of good will among all Canadians.
Experience has taught me that I should never enter into a debate with those of the opposite sex.

speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the minister on the latter portion of her speech, but I take exception to the earlier portion in which she referred to debates in this House as being sterile. The only reason for debates in this House being sterile is the government's failure to act or to take the initiative on the basis of the advice offered during those debates.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), while he is a fine gentleman, stated on February 28 that more was accomplished in the first session of this parliament than would normally be accomplished in five or six years. My response to that observation is to express disappointment that the previous session produced so little, due to lack of leadership and good management by the the government. If parliament did such a good job in 1973 to the extent that it exceeded five or six years' work, it is not surprising that Canada is in its present state of distress and hardship. We must remember that 60 per cent of our current inflation of over 9 per cent has been induced by this government-in other words, over half-and all the mumbling and jumbling of words by government members to try to say otherwise cannot alter that fact.
Canadians are entitled to, and expect, efficient administration, but their hopes are fading fast, particularly when the cost of government itself continues to multiply without any attempt to cut expenditure or to consider the sacrifices many taxpayers are forced to make to meet tax demands. Let the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) remember that it was the taxation policy of government which divided and destroyed the 12 tribes of Israel and has destroyed empires since.
Let me give a few examples to illustrate the lack of planning, and mismanagement during the first session of the twenty-ninth parliament. When the crop insurance bill, Bill C-129, was presented to the House the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wanted it pushed through without debate. Apparently he does not have any idea of the requirements of an appropriate crop insurance scheme. It would be more sensible and just to leave that type of legislation to people who do know what is necessary to provide an adequate system of protection for farmers. Even the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) travelled across this country condemning members of the official opposition for questioning the bill, suggesting we were holding up its passage because we were asking the minister to consider our proposals which were sound and proper. Evidently he never intended to use any of our suggestions in spite of the fact that he knew they would have been of benefit to the Canadian producer.
The bill was passed in its original form, with the result that producers within the province of Ontario do not receive any extra protection for their crops, and those in other provinces gain very little. Bill C-129 certainly does not give the minister much on which to hang his hat, if through it he is supposed to improve production and protect the agricultural industry. It is to be hoped that legislation to be introduced during this session will be of a wider range and more in line with what is required.
The Address-Mr. Towers
In addition to the weaknesses of Bill C-129, the government failed to provide adequate policies on energy, agriculture, expansionism in industry and manufacturing, an efficient unemployment insurance program, transportation, and numerous other matters. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is of the opinion that the legislation introduced in the previous session reflects good government, he does not know what is required of government or of parliament and his feelings are very different from mine.
Government is probably the biggest business in Canada today. If any other business was administered on the basis on which this government is administered, its life would be very short indeed. I agree with the government member who said he would not stand for election in the next campaign because, he said, "I still happen to believe that no one, including government, should spend more than they take in". He said that his views were not fresh in this modern world. However, like the hon. member, I would rather be termed old-fashioned than disinterested, arrogant and unaware of the problems and wishes of the people I represent and of Canadians in general.
At the western economic opportunities conference, representatives of the federal government did not have anything to offer. All the western premiers knew the needs and desires of their provinces, but this government again failed to present any suggestions or ideas to meet their demands. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) did manage later on to set up a confrontation between his government and the province of Alberta on the energy issue by his irresponsible conduct and attitude. If the Prime Minister had been at all concerned about the interests of the provinces in this country and their retention of natural resources, he would have removed that minister from his portfolio.
During the national energy conference, the maritime provinces were justifiably disturbed by the discrepancy in the cost of energy to their provinces compared to that in the central, manufacturing area of Canada. The producing provinces were worried lest they would not receive value for their natural resources. I ask the Prime Minister whether he considers it just to take a natural resource-I am thinking primarily of oil-away from a province and then, before it is used, allow the provincial and federal governments to levy a tax on that product. It would seem to me reasonable that the producing areas should receive maximum value for their product and the federal government could find its revenue elsewhere.
The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board promised to bring in legislation which would provide an equitable selling price for feed grain across Canada, and at the same time correct the inconsistencies in freight rates. He did introduce a policy on grain, but he did not present any regulations to correct the freight rates situation. So until the next crop year the western producer of red meat is being placed at a severe disadvantage. Feed grains move east at Crowsnest rates, plus feed freight assistance; western meat goes east at regular domestic rates, leaving the western producer with a loss of approximately $5 per hog compared to his eastern counterpart. On an annual prairie production of four million hogs, this alone means a disparity of $20 million in the western provinces.

The Address-Mr. Towers
In the 1973 budget the federal government started to meddle with the beef industry by removing the import surcharge. Last August, without any warning and while parliament was not in session, this government created a chaotic situation for all beef producing provinces by imposing a surcharge on beef exported to the United States. This is another example of an inept government causing hardship through inconsiderate interference.
On that particular day I was having lunch with the manager of a western Canada packing plant. We knew that the cabinet was meeting to make a decision. When the manager asked me if I thought the federal government would impose controls, I said that I hoped not because there had already been too many government controls put into effect. My feeling was that such action would not achieve anything but would disrupt the industry, and that surely the Minister of Agriculture would be wise enough and would have sufficient influence on cabinet to prevent this move. I naturally thought that, should the government decide to place a tax on beef going to the United States, this would not come into effect in the middle of a week. However, as everyone knows, that is exactly what the government decided to do. It announced controls on beef exports late on Monday evening. That asinine move at an inopportune time cost producers of beef thousands and thousands of dollars. One man lost $5,000 on just one shipment. Had he not been deprived of that $5,000, it would have counteracted to a degree the losses he is experiencing today.
The Minister of Agriculture must know very well that there are many feed lots in western and eastern Canada which are only partially in use. Let me impress upon this government that there will be fewer animals in feed lots this coming year than there have been for a long time. People do not forget, nor can they overlook the careless handling of their very livelihood by a mismanaged government which panics and reaches decisions without regard for the implications and hardships which follow.
I would urge the government, for the benefit of all Canadians, to recognize the seriousness of the situation faced by the red meat industry. The inequity the government has created in the hog industry as between east and west has resulted in hog producers cutting down production. In the hog industry, apparently the proper ratio is the slaughter of one full grown sow to 20 market hogs. In the past several months the ratio has been one sow slaughtered to 13 market hogs-quite a cutback-which means that we will be short of pork in this country. The cattle industry is in the same position. People are fed up with the meddling and unnecessary interference, plus the lack of consideration and sound policy on the part of the federal government which would encourage production, at a time when the world is hungry and there is a 5 per cent shortfall in the production of grain.
Canada imported over 70 million pounds of beef last year. In 1974 the amount will no doubt be greater. In 1972 this country imported under 30 million pounds of butter. For 1973 the estimated figure is in the neighbourhood of 50 million pounds. Milk production dropped by 5 per cent last year also. Where does this government think it is leading the Canadian people, or where is it pushing them, when

we cannot even supply our own requirements, with all the potential and the ability that we possess to produce?
Problems within agriculture are mounting. Farm labour is in short supply and producers are becoming discouraged because the government does not care enough to provide an atmosphere in which the industry can survive. All we can do right now is to await with anticipation the legislation that the Minister of Agriculture is supposed to be bringing forth. But we in the official opposition wish to warn him now to take note that we will continue to scrutinize his proposals to see whether this time there is anything that can benefit the producer and consumer. When production decreases, the producer suffers and every consumer suffers. Vast numbers of Canadian consumers are now suffering and can only look to additional hardship as a result of the inefficiency of this leaderless, "don't care" government.
Why is this government not doing something now to alleviate the bottleneck in the grain industry? What does it need to see the light? Twelve ships are waiting at the west coast to load grain. The grain is not there. There will be ten more ships docking next week. Demurrage charges are mounting. Elevators are plugged. Farmers are anxious to move their grain before spring break-up and seeding commences. This government sits on its hands in Ottawa while the Wheat Board asks farms to deliver their grain. Anyone in the know realizes why there is frustration within the agricultural industry.
When the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) announced the current local initiatives program, he asked members of parliament to co-operate so that the program could fill the need in the most deserving areas. He requested advice on projects which would be most suitable. I know that some members would not have anything to do with this controversial program due to previous examples of poor judgment and abuse which they could not stop no matter how hard they tried. But I believed it to be my responsibility to try to offer some advice, to help my constituency and to help the minister. His request was complied with: a constituency advisory group was set up and there were several projects to submit. In November of 1973 I informed the minister, through his staff, of three projects that I considered to be worth while to the communities concerned, and I Informed him by letter directed to his office. These were projects from which there would be continuing benefit; in other words, the money would not have gone down the drain.
In order to try to get these three projects approved-and they do not go beyond the total allotted to my riding-I made numerous telephone calls and finally contacted a member of his staff. But I ran up against a stone wall and the three projects have not yet been accepted. On countless occasions calls were placed to the minister directly and the promise given that he would return my call. I am still waiting for that call. Four months have passed and I have not received an answer for my constituents. They are waiting and so am I. No other business could function or remain solvent under such sloppy management; and I do not conduct my constituency business in that manner either.
March 1, 1974

Add this frustration to that faced by producers, manufacturers, small businesses, the construction industry, the legitimately unemployed and you have a vague idea how a power-hungry, couldn't-care-less government carries out its duties and responsibilities.
The hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) gave sound advice to the government, but apparently they do not intend to follow his advice. What about inflation, anyway? Obviously, the government members do not have any proposals of their own to curb the rising cost of production. As an example, last winter we saw a rise of from 100 per cent to 150 per cent in the price of anti-freeze alone. We have seen a fearful rise in the cost of food. Sugar alone is up 50 per cent. What will this do to beekeepers who require vast quantities of sugar to provide for hives until the productive season commences? This perhaps will answer the question of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), who raised the same point this afternoon. I received a call from a constituent who will need 15 tons of sugar. What will this 50 per cent hike do to the price of honey?
A contractor asked me for information on the continually spiralling cost of construction material. He was considering a contract to extend over 18 months and involving $500,000, but was afraid to enter into a binding agreement without any control being placed on the skyrocketing rise in price for the material required.
Let me give you an example, Mr. Speaker, of the prices of different types of material. In December, 1973, the price of two-inch pipe per 100 feet was $112.50 in February of 1974 it was $211.20, a 90 per cent increase in price. Three-inch pipe in December was $150 per 100 feet; in February it had risen to $251.20. Four-inch pipe was $159 per 100 feet; in February it was $310. As I said, Mr. Speaker, that is a 90 per cent increase in four months. How can this contractor submit a contract and feel financially safe?
On top of that, there is a shortage of material. He normally orders 100 tons of sheet steel one year and 200 tons the next year. Normally he uses 150 tons of steel. In January, February and March he ordered 100 tons of steel; he received no allotment. For April, May and June he ordered another 100 tons of steel; he was allotted 40 tons. How can these people survive in conditions such as this and with a government that stands idly by and allows this sort of thing to take place? What can such soaring costs do but hamper home construction, industry, in fact any type of business, not to mention the wage earner who finds
The Address-Mr. Towers
himself with less to spare for food and other necessities of life as each month goes by?
We all know how important it is for a young couple to be able to acquire their own home. At today's prices, most newly married couples cannot even save the down payment. And if they are fortunate enough to squeeze out the down payment after much scrimping and sacrifice, they cannot meet the monthly payments. When they look ahead and realize that they will be paying three or four times the contract price for their home due to high interest charges, life immediately becomes less interesting and they have a feeling that they will be plodding to pay for most of their lives. If homes were available at decent or reasonable amounts there would be fewer social problems. Young families should not be compelled to live under circumstances that place pressures on marriages and where children enter the world with unhappy, disillusioned parents.
Surveys conducted on crime have revealed that the majority of offenders come from environments of uncertainty, and in some cases have parents who were burdened beyond their ability to meet the demands that society had placed upon them. Those of us who have never had to stop to think about purchasing a home, or who have never felt insecure in our family life, perhaps cannot visualize what the day to day scrimping, worrying, never-ending anxieties can do to a person's general outlook. I do not think it would be unfair to say that the federal government could cut some of the many millions of dollars it now proposes to spend on government structures, which are certainly not needed. Renovations, expensive trappings for offices, multiplication of staff, uncalled for trips by government officials and public servants could total several million dollars.
Almost daily we have new reports of fantastic plans for growth in buildings and other government expenditures. I do not believe this is at all necessary at a time when so many taxpayers are finding it impossible to even purchase food and other daily requirements. A cutback in unnecessary government spending would be a step in the right direction. This is a step this government has never been prepared to take, but I hope that it will be taken during this second session of the twenty-ninth parliament. There must be a start some time-and it should be now during this serious time of inflation in the year 1974.
